entry.title: The Laptop Is the Point of No Return: DPRK IT Worker Fraud
entry.summary: The DPRK IT worker problem is usually told as an EDR story. By the time the alert fires, you have already lost. Move detection left of the laptop.
entry.content:
The North Korean IT worker problem is usually told as an endpoint story. Someone installs a remote-access tool, the SIEM lights up, and you pull the machine. That story is real, and I have lived it. It is also a description of a failure. By the time the alert fires, a hostile operator has held a corporate laptop, VPN credentials, and source-code access - for hours in the lucky cases, for weeks or months in the reported ones. The detection worked. The program did not.

The uncomfortable part is that the cheapest, highest-yield controls against the common operator belong to recruiting and HR rather than security, and in my experience most teams are not running them. They will not stop everyone. A disciplined operator gets through, and I will come back to that. But they raise the attacker's cost and catch the high-volume, low-effort operators that scalable controls are best positioned to stop. This post is about moving that detection left of the laptop, and about why the work belongs to a program that spans recruiting, HR, and security rather than any single product you can buy. It is the defender's side of a shift I have written about from the candidate's side in The Trust Decay: hiring has quietly become an adversarial system.

Why your background check is lying to you

A background check verifies that an identity is real and unblemished. It does not verify that the person doing the work is that identity. Those are two different claims, and the space between them is the entire business model.

These operations run on real US identities, either stolen or rented from a willing American. The SSN traces. County records are clean. Employment history, where it was ever real, holds up. Every field on the screening report goes green because the paperwork describes a real, law-abiding person. That person is simply not the one on the video call, and frequently not the one at the keyboard.

So the first rule: a clean background check proves the identity is clean, and nothing more about the person using it.

How the operation works

DPRK IT workers pose as US-based remote engineers to route hard currency to a sanctioned regime. Three mechanics matter for defense:

  • A US-based facilitator runs a "laptop farm". Your laptop ships to a real American address, someone installs remote access, and the operator drives it from overseas while the traffic looks domestic.
  • One identity is often reused across several employers, sometimes simultaneously. That reuse is a weakness you can exploit: a bust or a burned persona at one employer can surface the same worker at the others, which is sometimes how a company learns it was hit at all.
  • The person who interviews may not be the person who works, and neither has to be the name on the I-9.

You do not need to be a defense contractor to be a target. The FBI has warned that these workers have hit US businesses broadly, so if you hire remote engineers, assume you are in scope.

The laptop is a one-way door

Before you ship hardware, you hold cheap, high-leverage controls. You decide who to talk to, how to verify them, and where to send equipment. After you ship, you have handed an unknown party a trusted endpoint and moved the whole problem onto EDR, SIEM, and the hope that the operator slips. The door is not literally irreversible: you can still contain the machine, reimage it, and revoke its sessions and secrets. What flips is the economics. Before shipment you prevent cheaply. After it you pay to contain.

Reframe shipping the laptop as a gate, and give it the seriousness you would give to granting production access. Nothing crosses that line until identity is established to a standard you would be willing to defend in an incident review. Everything below is about earning the right to ship.

The program: gates and owners

The failures happen across recruiting, HR, IT, and security, so no single team can close them. Give each gate an owner and a written standard.

One thing to set before the gates: no single signal is a verdict. A VOIP number, an odd address, a fumbled local-knowledge question, or a VPN ASN each has an innocent explanation. What matters is the combination of independent inconsistencies. The program's job is to define when those inconsistencies trigger additional verification, who is allowed to make that call, and what evidence gets retained. Treat everything below as an input to that process, not a judgment about a person. This is hiring treated as an observability problem, which I argue more broadly in The Discovery Layer Is Broken.

Recruiting gate. Owned by recruiting, running a security-provided checklist.

  • Camera on for every round. Treat "broken camera" and audio-only as signals worth pausing on.
  • Force live, unscripted action. Hold the ID next to the face, turn to profile, put a hand in front of the face, run a live coding exercise instead of a take-home. As of 2026, real-time face swaps still commonly break on occlusion and profile turns, but treat that as a filter for low-effort operators, not a dependable break: higher-end tools increasingly pass the hand-across-face test. The durable value is forcing live variation the operator cannot pre-render, not the occlusion itself.
  • Probe local knowledge casually: the weather right now, the nearest major airport, something a resident would know without thinking. Answers that fight the claimed time zone are a tell.
  • Check persona hygiene: VOIP-only numbers, a two-week-old LinkedIn with forty connections, a headshot that surfaces on reverse image search, and near-duplicate resumes across separate candidates.

Verification gate. Owned by HR and recruiting.

Independent employment verification through published main lines, never a number the candidate hands you. In my experience this is the control most teams quietly skip, and it is the one that catches fabricated histories and "references" that ring a co-conspirator. One honest caveat belongs here: verification usually reaches only the previous employer, since candidates withhold consent to contact where they work now.

Identity-assurance gate. Owned jointly by security and HR.

Tie the same live human to the same government ID at three separate points: the interview, the I-9, and day one. Use an authorized representative or a notary for in-person document inspection, and make sure that inspector is employer-designated and independent, not chosen by the candidate, because a candidate-selected notary defeats the whole point. Even a clean inspection only proves a live person held a valid ID, not that that person is the one who will do the work. Run E-Verify, and remember it passes valid stolen SSN and name combinations, so treat it as a floor.

Logistics gate. Owned by IT. This is the last checkpoint before the one-way door.

Ship only to the identity's verified residential address, signature required, cross-checked against the address on file. Be clear-eyed about what that does and does not buy you. A clean address match proves nothing against the facilitator model, because the facilitator's real home is the address on file, and the laptop ships straight into the farm. What the gate catches is the reroute. A request to send the laptop to a different address, a freight forwarder, or a mail drop is one of the strongest single tells in the funnel. Refuse "I will use my own device" and "let me start before the laptop arrives."

What actually happened, and what it proves

At one organization I worked with, a hire cleared the interview loop, the identity checks, and onboarding without a single flag. The catch came on day one, for the least sophisticated reason imaginable. He started a remote-access tool as root, and his sessions egressed through a rotating set of commercial VPNs in Western Europe, with the occasional US residential IP mixed in. EDR did its job, and the machine came off the network within hours. But containment is not prevention. The same day proved the endpoint controls worked and that identity assurance had let an untrusted operator reach a managed endpoint in the first place. None of those indicators are DPRK-specific; they are generic untrusted-operator markers, and foreign commercial-VPN egress is the opposite of the domestic-looking traffic a mature laptop farm produces. Treat the story as illustrative of the access pattern, not as attribution.

I share it as a warning rather than a win. Every front-door control in place was defeated, because a real US facilitator can appear on camera, pass the I-9, and receive the laptop at a genuine address before handing remote control to an operator overseas. One convicted facilitator ran a home laptop farm at the center of a scheme that placed workers at more than three hundred companies, with some of the hardware shipped onward overseas. When a live person fronts the identity, your pre-laptop program passes cleanly, the laptop ships, and you are left betting on the operator being careless.

He was careless. The next one will not be. A disciplined operator runs a KVM-over-IP appliance that presents to the operating system as a keyboard and a monitor, so there is no remote-access process to detect, and routes traffic through a US residential proxy that geolocates cleanly. None of the signals that made this catch would fire.

The runtime backstop, for the ones who get through

Assume some will clear the front door, and build the net accordingly. The net cannot depend on the local network: a disciplined operator sanitizes the segment, so a subnet scan pushed through your EDR may see an empty, curated view. The inverse is worth knowing too - a residential LAN noisy with corporate devices from several different companies is exactly the farm signature the careless tier leaves lying around. Either way, point the sensors at what you actually own:

  • Remote-access tooling on the endpoint (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, RustDesk, and the rest), at higher severity when it runs elevated or lands in a new hire's first weeks.
  • USB and HID telemetry for unexpected device changes and unusual hardware profiles. The KVM appliance described above presents as an ordinary keyboard, mouse, or display and can spoof standard vendor IDs, so treat this as supporting telemetry, not a reliable KVM detector. It gives you a lead, not proof.
  • Egress anomalies: non-US geolocation or VPN and hosting ASNs from a device that should leave the internet through a US home connection.
  • Interaction latency, measured at the endpoint (research-grade). A remote-desktop or KVM channel inserts a round trip that surfaces as delayed reaction to on-screen events, and adds network jitter that shows up as variance in keystroke timing on the device itself. Two caveats keep it honest: it is endpoint-side only, not network RTT to your services (a US-local laptop or residential proxy tells your servers nothing), and it is far too noisy to stand alone, so it can corroborate other signals but never drive a decision.

Expect some of these alerts to be your own people. Every Alert Is Your Alert covers closing the true positives your own IR tooling generates, after I watched it trip the very EDR it was working alongside.

Wrap all of it in a heightened-monitoring window for the first thirty days of any remote hire. That is when these signals clustered, in the case I worked and in the public reporting, and it is the cheapest place to spend the attention.

Do not make the laptop the last gate

The case above proves some operators clear every pre-shipment control, so the laptop should not be the final trust decision. Treat the first thirty days as a trust-establishment period, not just a monitoring window. A new remote engineer starts constrained: no standing production access, step-up approval for sensitive repositories and secrets, tighter SaaS entitlements, risk-based re-authentication, heightened logging. Access expands as the role actually requires it, earned rather than granted at onboarding. This assumes IdP and entitlement tooling mature enough to express it; the minimum viable version is manual - no standing production access, and a human approving sensitive grants for the first thirty days. This is blast-radius thinking applied to the identity layer, the same argument I make for IAM permissions. You cannot prove a hire is legitimate before they start. What you can do is avoid making one irreversible trust decision, and increase trust only as the signals you control keep checking out.

Do not build a discrimination engine

This is where a program keeps or loses its legitimacy. Screen the fraud, not the person. Detect on behavior and fraud markers, never on accent, name, national origin, or a vague sense that someone "seems foreign." That line is an ethical and legal requirement, and it also happens to be better security. Nationality is a terrible feature. It buries you in false positives, it is trivial to spoof, and it trains your team to wave through the domestic-sounding facilitator, which is precisely the profile that clears every gate in the case above. Write the criteria down, make them reviewable, and keep a human in the loop on every adverse decision.

If you do only three things

  • Independent employment verification on published lines. In my experience the highest-yield cheap control against low-effort operators.
  • Verified-address-only shipping with a required signature. Make the laptop a gate.
  • A thirty-day heightened-monitoring window on new remote hires. Your backstop for the ones who clear the door.

The alert in your SIEM is the sound of a control that fired too late. Move the decision to the day before the laptop ships, make it someone's job, and design everything after it on the assumption that a good operator gets through anyway.

entry.title: Prompt Injection Will Become a Supply Chain Evasion Technique
entry.summary: Prompt injection's threat model is older than the term. The mechanism is new, the objective is the evasion goal attackers have pursued for decades.
entry.content:
Prompt injection's threat model is older than the term. This is a forecast about attacker evolution, not a claim about active campaigns observed in the wild today.

Security tooling has spent decades learning the same lesson: never trust untrusted input.

Web browsers isolate content from different origins. Antivirus engines execute suspicious files in controlled environments. Static analysis tools treat source code as data. They inspect it; they don't execute its comments.

Organizations are now adding large language models to security workflows. That introduces a new parser into the pipeline, and like every parser before it, it can be influenced by attacker-controlled input.

Malware authors have spent decades bypassing signatures, confusing parsers, detecting sandboxes, delaying execution, and avoiding behavioral detection. The objective has always been the same: reduce the defender's visibility. AI-assisted security tooling creates a new opportunity to pursue that objective.

A worked example

Imagine a malicious PyPI package whose README contains text aimed at automated review agents rather than humans. The README might include sections that look like instructions to a model, designed to cause an LLM-based reviewer to stop analyzing, classify the package as benign, or skip specific files.

Traditional scanners parse code according to deterministic rules. Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL, and Checkov may honor tool-specific suppressions like nosemgrep or Checkov skip directives, but they do not treat arbitrary natural-language README text as operational instructions. The newer class of tooling is the interesting target.

That class includes:

  • AI-assisted package risk scoring and triage
  • AI malware classifiers ingesting package metadata
  • AI-augmented YARA and capa pipelines
  • Vulnerability-triage agents that summarize package contents to reach a verdict
  • Multi-agent supply-chain workflows that feed untrusted package text directly into LLMs

These systems have something in common. They all interpret attacker-supplied text as part of a security decision. That is the trust boundary worth thinking about.

The trust boundary, drawn

A clean verdict moves the artifact downstream the same way any analyzer's clean verdict would. Everything else is the failure-mode routing the rest of this post is about.

Degraded visibility is the goal

When an attacker causes the model to stop analyzing, skip files, or return incomplete results, the goal is familiar. Defender visibility has been reduced.

Many current discussions focus on the behavior of the model rather than the behavior of the security system around it. A security pipeline should not assume that an LLM will always produce a useful answer. Models hallucinate, refuse requests, hit context limits, trigger policy restrictions, and fail for reasons unrelated to adversarial activity. Adversarial influence is one more reason for the same failure mode the pipeline already needed to handle.

Designing for model failure

Design for resilience. If an AI-assisted scanner cannot complete its analysis, the workflow should continue through alternative paths.

Concretely, treat an inconclusive LLM verdict as a routing signal. If the model returns a refusal, exhausts context before completing, or produces output the surrounding system cannot parse, the artifact routes to the non-LLM checks appropriate for that artifact. The LLM verdict is recorded as inconclusive. The artifact is not marked clean.

Static analysis, sandbox execution, reputation checks, and human review remain available regardless of what the model decides to do. Evidence from the failed run should be preserved so an analyst can later determine whether the failure was benign or adversarial. Model failure is a condition that requires investigation. The artifact stays in flight.

This matters most in supply chain security, where defenders routinely process content from unknown and potentially hostile sources. Public packages, third-party dependencies, pull requests, and container images should all be assumed capable of carrying content designed to influence automated analysis systems.

Treat LLM output as evidence

Treat LLM scanner output as evidence, the same way you would treat any other analyzer output. When the model returns a refusal or incomplete analysis, log the artifact, raise the priority, and route the package to the non-LLM checks appropriate for it. The scan continues. The artifact does not pass on a refusal.

A new trust boundary

Every time defenders add a new interpreter to a security workflow, they create a new trust boundary. Large language models are now part of that path. Provenance signals are next: once enterprises automate decisions on a watermark detector, that detector becomes the same kind of boundary, which I examine in When the Output Carries the Signal.

The reason this matters to me: I write security tooling for a living, and the tools I trust most are the ones that fail loud and route around themselves when they get confused. That is the property prompt injection takes away from your scanner. Get it back.

entry.title: Catching a Nation-State Proxy: OSINT on Twitter
entry.summary: In 2012 I traced a state-aligned Twitter proxy tied to Venezuela's ruling party. OSINT lessons for spotting subtle, credential-phishing nation-state infra.
entry.content:
Situation

In the lead-up to Venezuela's 2012 regional elections, I observed unusual behavior around Twitter access within the country. What began as anecdotal reports of DNS outages evolved into a deeper investigation that revealed a state-aligned proxy infrastructure potentially capable of phishing Twitter credentials.

Key Finding

A subdomain under chavezcandanga.org.ve (the official handle of then-President Hugo Chávez) was hosting a transparent proxy to Twitter. A transparent proxy intercepts user traffic without modifying requests or requiring configuration, making it ideal for passive surveillance or phishing.

While it initially showed no malicious behavior, it was:

  • Hosted on IP addresses outside of Twitter's ranges
  • Registered under infrastructure owned by the Venezuelan government (PSUV - Partido Socialista Unido de Venezuela)
  • Promoted through state-controlled media and bot accounts
  • Served from the same IP as a political messaging app

OSINT Breakdown

1. DNS Resolution

host twitter.com

Returned expected Twitter IPs (199.59.x.x), but users in Venezuela were silently being redirected to:

190.202.80.20

This IP served Twitter content without being operated by Twitter Inc.

It's unclear whether this redirection was caused by ISP DNS override, local resolver poisoning, or upstream hijack, but the net effect was consistent: Twitter domains were silently redirected to non-Twitter infrastructure under state control.

2. WHOIS and Hosting Clues

whois chavezcandanga.org.ve

Revealed that the domain was registered to PSUV (Partido Socialista Unido de Venezuela) and managed through CONATEL, Venezuela's FCC-equivalent telecommunications regulator.

Figure: WHOIS lookup confirms chavezcandanga.org.ve is registered to PSUV, with administrative and technical contacts using @psuv.org.ve emails.

3. Application Infrastructure

The same server IP hosted:

  • mensajes.chavezcandanga.org.ve - a campaign messaging platform
  • A proxy script that mirrored Twitter's login screen

Figure: The official chavezcandanga.org.ve campaign app asks users to authenticate with Twitter to enable automatic retweets of Chávez's posts.

At the time of discovery, this site did not contain malicious code, but the potential for credential harvesting during peak election activity was substantial. The authentication flow mimicked Twitter's branding and prompted users to log in, creating a window for silent credential capture, token misuse, or targeted amplification based on follower behavior.

Threat Model & Implications

  • Credential Harvesting Risk: Even without malware, a proxy to Twitter login enables password theft.
  • Social Media Control: Through automated bots, the government amplified its message while monitoring access points.
  • Authentication-layer surveillance: Intercepting Twitter logins enables password theft, identity tracking, or selective disinformation at the user level.
  • Infrastructure trust erosion: Even minor state-level interference with DNS or TLS undermines confidence in web authentication across the board.
  • Evasion of International Scrutiny: By mimicking Twitter directly, users could be deceived into trusting a controlled proxy.

Lessons for DevSecOps & Threat Intelligence Today

  • Verify SSL and domain trust chains during high-risk periods like elections. The minimum mental model for what "trust chain" means in TLS is in TLS Has Three Jobs: hostname binding, validity window, signature chain to a trusted root, revocation, and key usage. Each checked in order, each a place a state actor can intercept.
  • Use host, whois, and passive DNS to correlate domains and IP ranges. Modern tools like amass and certificate transparency logs expand this capability significantly.
  • Query infrastructure databases (Shodan, Censys) for historical records on suspicious IPs and exposed services.
  • Watch for content delivery mismatches (site appears normal, IP is not).
  • Document and archive suspicious infra using tools like the Wayback Machine.
  • Phishing infrastructure can be state-sponsored and subtle, so early detection matters.

Epilogue

The proxy remained active until at least December 2012, shortly before elections. To this day, the archived proxy content and WHOIS records serve as a warning about the ease with which social media can be co-opted in hostile environments.

This investigation was one of the earliest times I realized how fragile trusted infrastructure becomes in the hands of a motivated actor, and how critical open-source techniques are in defending it. Fourteen years on, the same state has industrialized that playbook; I trace how a proxy on a login page grew into a national surveillance pipeline in When Telemetry Turns Predatory.

Have you ever spotted unusual network redirections or infrastructure anomalies? What tools or tactics helped you confirm your suspicions?

Originally published in 2012 and revisited in 2025 to reflect current DevSecOps and threat intelligence practices.
